relations.myth: Vāyu emerges from the cosmic Person’s breath
relations.note: Vāyu or wind arises from Puruṣa’s breath in a late Vedic cosmogony.

relations.myth: Purāṇic creation of Vāyu
relations.note: Some Purāṇic accounts incorporate Vāyu into creation by Brahmā.

relations.myth: Wind generates fire in elemental creation
relations.note: The elemental sequence states that wind arises from ether and generates fire.

relations.myth: Kuntī invokes Vāyu and conceives Bhīma
relations.note: The epic presents Vāyu as Bhīma’s divine father and source of his strength.

relations.myth: Vāyu’s second salvific descent
relations.note: Dvaita theology identifies Bhīma as Vāyu’s second incarnation serving Kṛṣṇa.

relations.myth: Vāyu engenders or empowers Añjanā’s son
relations.note: Hanumān is Vāyu’s divine or spiritual son, equal to him in speed and power.

relations.myth: Vāyu withdraws air after Hanumān is struck
relations.note: Vāyu suffocates the worlds until the gods revive and bless the injured Hanumān.

relations.myth: Vāyu’s first salvific descent
relations.note: Dvaita theology identifies Hanumān as Vāyu’s first incarnation and Rāma’s servant.

relations.myth: Maruts born from Vāyu’s belly
relations.note: An isolated Vedic genealogy says the Maruts arise from Vāyu’s belly.

relations.myth: Shared sacrificial and atmospheric invocations
relations.note: Vāyu and the Maruts appear together in sacrificial and atmospheric contexts.

relations.myth: Indrāvāyū share Soma and a chariot
relations.note: Vāyu and Indra arrive jointly and receive the first Soma pressing.

relations.myth: Indra earns a share of Vāyu’s cup
relations.note: Vāyu’s formerly exclusive Soma cup is shared with Indra as payment for service.

relations.myth: Indra wounds Hanumān and Vāyu withdraws air
relations.note: After Indra strikes Hanumān, Vāyu withholds breath until the gods placate him.

relations.myth: Vāyu receives Soma’s first draught
relations.note: Pressed and purified Soma is poured expressly for Vāyu to drink first.

relations.myth: Fire and wind coordinate across cosmic regions
relations.note: Agni and Vāyu are coordinated as terrestrial and atmospheric cosmic powers.

relations.myth: Fire resolves into Vāyu
relations.note: In the absorber doctrine, fire is gathered or resolved into cosmic Vāyu.

relations.myth: Sun and wind form cosmic counterparts
relations.note: Later Vedic systems correlate celestial Sūrya with atmospheric Vāyu and cosmic Prāṇa.

relations.myth: Hanumān seeks instruction from Sūrya
relations.note: Vāyu’s relation to Sūrya is mediated through his son Hanumān’s later education.

relations.myth: Speech challenges the supremacy of breath
relations.note: Speech can depart without killing the body but fails when chief breath prepares to leave.

relations.myth: Faculties dispute supremacy with Prāṇa
relations.note: The faculties survive one another’s departure but are uprooted when Prāṇa attempts to leave.

relations.myth: Brahmā appeases Vāyu after Hanumān’s injury
relations.note: Brahmā helps revive and bless Hanumān, ending Vāyu’s withdrawal of cosmic breath.

relations.myth: Vāyu serves as Viṣṇu’s chief mediator
relations.note: Madhva theology ranks Vāyu beneath Viṣṇu as his perfect servant and salvific mediator.

relations.myth: Hanumān accompanies and serves Rāma
relations.note: Vāyu serves Viṣṇu’s Rāma incarnation through his first descent, Hanumān.

relations.myth: Bhīma executes Kṛṣṇa’s purpose
relations.note: Vāyu serves Kṛṣṇa through his second descent, Bhīma.

relations.myth: Madhva meets Vyāsa and receives instruction
relations.note: Vāyu’s third incarnation Madhva receives authoritative instruction from Vyāsa.

relations.myth: Vāyu’s third salvific descent
relations.note: Dvaita tradition identifies Madhva as Vāyu’s third incarnation and teacher of Vedānta.

relations.myth: Rudra’s power is transmitted through Vāyu
relations.note: Some Śaiva accounts make Hanumān Rudra’s manifestation while Vāyu carries or transmits the power.

relations.myth: Vāyu and Vāsuki struggle around a mountain
relations.note: Vāyu’s wind tears away a mountain peak during a strength contest with Vāsuki.

relations.myth: Vāyu assaults and breaks a mountain peak
relations.note: Epic and Purāṇic variants describe Vāyu breaking or moving peaks with his force.

relations.myth: Ahura Mazdā petitions Vayu for victory
relations.note: Iranian Vayu receives Ahura Mazdā’s sacrifice or petition and grants martial victory.

relations.myth: Vayu moves between the rival creations
relations.note: Iranian Vayu operates in the intermediate space between the good and evil creations.

relations.myth: Vayu moves between the rival creations
relations.note: Iranian Vayu operates in the intermediate space between the good and evil creations.

relations.myth: Vayu refuses a destructive petitioner
relations.note: Aži Dahāka petitions Vayu for victory, but Vayu refuses destructive claimants.
Early hymns distinguish Vāta from Vāyu, but later lexicons and mythography merge them.
Later systems correlate Vāyu with vital breath; Madhva identifies Mukhya-prāṇa as the conscious deity Vāyu.
Indian Vāyu entered East Asian Buddhism as the directional or elemental deity Fūten.
Wēšparkar is an eastern-Iranian development possibly connected with Vayu uparō.kairyō.
